cues.text: A Convert's Fragile Health
Agnes Sasagawa , a Japanese convert to Catholicism from Buddhism, entered the Institute of the Handmaids of the Sacred Heart of Jesus in the Holy Eucharist at Yuzawadai, near Akita, in May 1973.
She arrived already in fragile health, having suffered a paralysis in earlier years and lost her hearing only months before entering religious life.

Within weeks of her arrival, the small community's convent chapel became the setting for a series of extraordinary reported events centered on a simple wooden statue of Our Lady, carved from a single block of katsura wood.

The Institute itself was a small, relatively new community devoted especially to Eucharistic adoration, a charism that would come to seem, in hindsight, closely bound up with the very message the sisters would soon find themselves entrusted with.
Rays of Light, and a Wound in the Hand
In June 1973, Sister Agnes reported witnessing brilliant, unexplained rays of light emanating from the chapel's tabernacle on three consecutive days.
On June 28, a cross-shaped wound appeared on the inside of her left hand, bleeding painfully; the wound remained, by the sisters' own record, until it disappeared that September.
On July 6, several sisters present in the chapel reported the wooden statue's own right hand bleeding as well, an occurrence that repeated itself on four separate occasions.
The Statue Speaks

On that same day, July 6, 1973, Sister Agnes reported hearing a voice she attributed to the statue itself, delivering a message of prayer and reparation; two further messages followed, on August 3 and October 13 of that year.
The October message, the most detailed of the three, spoke of coming chastisement for a world grown indifferent to sin.
It also promised that prayer and penance, offered with sincerity, could still lessen its severity—a message the community immediately reported to their bishop rather than treat as a private matter.
A Hundred and One Tears
Beginning in January 1975 and continuing intermittently until 1981, the statue was witnessed weeping on 101 separate occasions altogether, by the sisters' own careful count.
The tears were captured on videotape by a Japanese television crew and broadcast nationally.
Hundreds of visitors, including the local bishop himself, reported witnessing the phenomenon firsthand.

When scientifically analyzed at the University of Akita, samples of the tears and blood were found consistent with genuine human fluid, a finding the diocese would later cite as part of its own careful investigation.
Eight Years of Investigation
Bishop John Shojiro Ito of Niigata, within whose diocese Akita fell, personally witnessed the statue's tears on more than one occasion.
He initiated a lengthy formal inquiry lasting the better part of a decade, drawing on theological consultation, scientific testing, and extensive interviews with witnesses.
On April 22, 1984, Bishop Ito issued a pastoral letter formally declaring the events supernatural in origin.
He authorized devotion to "the Holy Mother of Akita" throughout his diocese, stating plainly that what he and hundreds of others had witnessed could not be explained by any human contrivance.
Bishop Ito's own caution before reaching this judgment was considerable.
He consulted extensively with Rome and with theologians competent in the discernment of private revelation.
He was unwilling to move faster than the evidence itself could responsibly carry him.
Legacy
Sister Agnes's own reported deafness, which the apparition's messages had promised would be healed, lifted temporarily in 1974 and then permanently in 1982.
She remained a quiet, largely unassuming member of her small religious community for the rest of her long life.
She died in 2024 at ninety-three, on the very feast of the Assumption.
Akita remains one of the few Marian phenomena of the modern era to receive full diocesan approval.

Its message — a call to prayer, penance, and reparation offered not in dramatic public spectacle but through one convert-novice's quiet, hidden suffering — still draws pilgrims to a small Japanese convent.
Its own sisters, for many years, never expected the wider world to notice it at all.
